passage:
The architecture of forgetting

Cities often treat memory as an inventory: monuments preserve celebrated events, plaques identify exemplary citizens, and museums arrange the past into a sequence that appears settled. Yet urban memory is less like an archive than a negotiation. A demolished market may survive in the habits of vendors who relocate; a disused railway line may persist as a corridor in the city's mental map. Conversely, a monument can remain physically present while its meaning is quietly abandoned. The built environment therefore does not simply store history. It selects, edits and sometimes contradicts the stories residents tell about themselves. Planning authorities frequently describe redevelopment as the replacement of obsolete uses by more efficient ones. This vocabulary is not neutral. It makes displacement sound like technical housekeeping and turns contested social claims into questions of land utilisation. But preserving every structure is neither possible nor desirable. The more difficult task is to recognise that demolition is also an act of authorship: it determines which traces will remain available to future interpretation. A city that remembers responsibly need not freeze its streets; it must, however, make visible the choices through which its past is continually rewritten.

options: Monuments and museums are the most reliable means by which cities store their history.
Because a city’s fabric shapes what its past means, decisions to demolish or preserve should be recognised and made visible as choices about memory.
Redevelopment is a neutral technical process of replacing obsolete land uses with efficient ones.
Cities should preserve every historic structure so that residents do not lose touch with their past.
explanation: The author argues that the built environment “selects, edits and sometimes contradicts” history, rejects total preservation, and asks that the choices be made visible. B is explicitly rejected; C and D are views the author questions. From the CAT 2026 Original Advanced Question Bank (cleaned and verified).

label: VARC › Reading Comprehension › Main idea / Title
passage:
The limits of prediction

Prediction is often confused with understanding because both produce statements about what has not yet happened. A model may forecast demand with impressive accuracy while remaining silent about why consumers behave as they do. This distinction matters when conditions change. A model trained on stable patterns can become brittle precisely when decision-makers most need guidance. Yet the opposite error is to dismiss prediction as intellectually shallow. Forecasts can discipline intuition, expose hidden assumptions and reveal the consequences of uncertainty. The appropriate question is not whether a model understands the world in a human sense, but whether its errors are visible, bounded and consequentially manageable. Institutions often prefer a single forecast because it appears to simplify responsibility. A range of scenarios, by contrast, forces them to acknowledge that choices depend on values as well as probabilities. The most useful forecast may therefore be one that refuses to masquerade as certainty.
prompt: Which title best suits the passage?
options: Why Predictive Models Should Be Abandoned
Useful Forecasts: Valuing Prediction Without Mistaking It for Certainty
Accuracy as the Only Test of a Good Model
How Consumers Really Make Decisions
explanation: The passage defends prediction against dismissal while warning against treating it as understanding or certainty. B and C each take one extreme the author rejects; D is a detail. From the CAT 2026 Original Advanced Question Bank (cleaned and verified).

label: VARC › Reading Comprehension › Main idea / Title
passage:
The economics of attention

Attention is routinely described as though it were a commodity that can be transferred intact from one object to another. But attention is also a capacity shaped by the conditions under which it is exercised. A notification does not merely take seconds from a task; it can alter the mental context in which the task was being pursued. Platforms optimise measurable engagement because duration and frequency are legible to their systems. The quality of attention—whether it is reflective, fragmented, curious or coerced—is harder to quantify. This does not mean that all interruption is harmful or that sustained concentration is always virtuous. Some tasks benefit from rapid switching, and some forms of browsing generate unexpected connections. The problem arises when a metric designed to approximate attention becomes a substitute for the human purposes that made attention valuable in the first place.

explanation: The final sentence states the problem: a metric that approximates attention “becomes a substitute for the human purposes”. B and D are positions the author disowns; C overstates. From the CAT 2026 Original Advanced Question Bank (cleaned and verified).

label: VARC › Reading Comprehension › Main idea / Title
passage:
When maps become arguments

A map appears to describe territory, but every map also advances a theory of relevance. A transport map exaggerates some distances and suppresses others; a risk map converts uncertain events into coloured zones; a historical map chooses which boundaries deserve emphasis. Such simplification is unavoidable, since a map that represented everything would represent nothing intelligibly. The ethical question is therefore not whether maps distort, but who chooses the distortion and who bears its consequences. A flood-risk map may protect property owners while rendering informal settlements statistically invisible if its data omit unregistered dwellings. In this case, technical precision within the chosen dataset can coexist with profound representational failure. Better mapping requires not only improved instruments but scrutiny of categories, omissions and the decisions that follow.

explanation: The author accepts that distortion is unavoidable and shifts the ethical question to “who chooses the distortion and who bears its consequences”. C is explicitly rejected. From the CAT 2026 Original Advanced Question Bank (cleaned and verified).
